claim: The kinetic proofreading (KPR) model proposes that T cells discriminate self from foreign ligands by the different ligand binding half-lives to the T cell receptor (TCR).
source: The kinetic proofreading (KPR) model proposes that T cells discriminate self from foreign ligands by the different ligand binding half-lives to the T cell receptor (TCR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the KPR model, which is an established theoretical framework in the field.

claim: PhyB continuously cycles between the binding and non-binding states under red light, with the light intensity determining the cycling rate and thus the binding duration.
source: This opto-ligand-TCR system was combined with the unique property of PhyB to continuously cycle between the binding and non-binding states under red light, with the light intensity determining the cycling rate and thus the binding duration.
evidence: This is a key property of PhyB that is stated in the abstract and is central to the experimental design.

claim: Mathematical modeling of experimental datasets showed that the ligand-TCR interaction half-life is the decisive factor for activating downstream TCR signaling, substantiating KPR.
source: Mathematical modeling of our experimental datasets showed that indeed the ligand-TCR interaction half-life is the decisive factor for activating downstream TCR signaling, substantiating KPR.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by the combination of experimental data and mathematical modeling presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Foreign pMHCs bind with higher affinity to the TCR than non-stimulatory pMHC.
source: This discrimination between foreign and self pMHC correlates with the affinity of the ligand-TCR interaction, in that foreign, stimulatory pMHCs bind with higher affinity to the TCR than non-stimulatory pMHC (Davis et al., 1998; Sykulev et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Davis et al., 1998; Sykulev et al., 1994).

claim: In KPR, a long half-life of the ligand-TCR interaction allows a series of biochemical reactions to be completed that eventually trigger downstream signaling.
source: The KPR model proposes that a long half-life of the ligand-TCR interaction, such as seen for high affinity pMHC, allows a series of biochemical reactions to be completed that eventually trigger downstream signaling.
evidence: This is a description of the KPR model mechanism as stated in the introduction.

claim: A low affinity ligand detaches before an activatory signal is produced and the TCR then reverts quickly to the initial inactive state.
source: By contrast, a low affinity ligand detaches before an activatory signal is produced and the TCR then reverts quickly to the initial inactive state, thus not initiating T cell activation.
evidence: This is part of the KPR model description in the introduction.

claim: The on-rate plays a role in ligand discrimination if it is very fast, allowing rapid rebinding before biochemical reactions are reverted.
source: Although the half-life is the decisive factor, it was recently shown that the on-rate also plays a role (Aleksic et al., 2010; Govern et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2019). If the on-rate is very fast a ligand that has detached can rapidly rebind to the same TCR before the first biochemical reactions are reverted.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work (Aleksic et al., 2010; Govern et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2019).

claim: T cells are sensitive to low numbers of ligands (1–10 molecules).
source: At the same time, the high sensitivity of the T cells towards low numbers of ligands (1–10 molecules) was retained (Irvine et al., 2002; Purbhoo et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Irvine et al., 2002; Purbhoo et al., 2004).

claim: PhyB switches to its ON state upon illumination with 660 nm light and interacts with PIF6 with nanomolar affinity.
source: Upon illumination with 660 nm light, PhyB switches to its ON state in which it interacts with PIF6 with a nanomolar affinity (Levskaya et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Levskaya et al., 2009.

claim: With 740 nm light, PhyB undergoes a conformational transition to the OFF state preventing binding to PIF6.
source: With 740 nm light, PhyB undergoes a conformational transition to the OFF state preventing binding to PIF6.
evidence: This is a known property of PhyB stated in the introduction.

claim: The PhyB-PIF interaction can be switched ON and OFF within seconds using high intensity light.
source: Using high intensity light, the PhyB-PIF interaction can be switched ON and OFF within seconds (Levskaya et al., 2009; Mancinelli, 1994; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Levskaya et al., 2009; Mancinelli, 1994; Smith et al., 2016).

claim: At continuous 660 nm illumination, individual PhyB molecules constantly switch between the ON and OFF states in the order of seconds.
source: Importantly for our study, at continuous 660 nm illumination the individual PhyB molecules constantly switch between the ON and OFF states, again in the order of seconds, thus being within the range of the estimated KPR times (Mancinelli, 1994; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Mancinelli, 1994; Smith et al., 2016).

claim: Chimeric TCRs with binding domains fused to the ectodomain of TCRβ were expressed on the cell surface and were activated via the appended binding domains.
source: We and others have previously fused binding domains to the ectodomain of the TCRβ subunit; either a single chain Fv fragment (Minguet et al., 2007) or a single strand DNA oligonucleotide (Taylor et al., 2017). Indeed, the chimeric TCRs were expressed on the cell surface and were activated via the appended binding domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Minguet et al., 2007; Taylor et al., 2017).

claim: Ligand discrimination occurred when using the DNA-TCR, where a low affinity binder did not evoke TCR stimulation and a high affinity binder did.
source: Importantly, ligand discrimination also occurred when using the DNA-TCR; i.e., a low affinity binder to the DNA did not evoke TCR stimulation and a high affinity binder did (Taylor et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Taylor et al., 2017.

claim: Ligands do not need to bind to the canonical pMHC binding site within the TCR for ligand discrimination to occur.
source: This clearly showed that ligands do not need to bind to the canonical pMHC binding site within the TCR and that co-receptors are not required for ligand discrimination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the DNA-TCR experiments cited (Taylor et al., 2017).

claim: Co-receptors are not required for ligand discrimination.
source: This clearly showed that ligands do not need to bind to the canonical pMHC binding site within the TCR and that co-receptors are not required for ligand discrimination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the DNA-TCR experiments cited (Taylor et al., 2017).

claim: 70% of PhyB molecules were complexed with PIF after illuminating a mixture of PhyB and excess MBP-PIF(wt) with saturating 660 nm light.
source: After illuminating a mixture of PhyB and an excess MBP-PIF(wt) with saturating 660 nm light, 70% of the PhyB molecules were complexed with PIF as depicted by a shift in elution from a size exclusion chromatography column (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At photoequilibrium under 660 nm light, only 80% of the PhyB molecules are in the ON state.
source: Since at photoequilibrium under 660 nm light only 80% of the PhyB molecules are in the ON state (Bae and Choi, 2008; Smith et al., 2016), we conclude that the majority of PhyB molecules were functionally active.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Bae and Choi, 2008; Smith et al., 2016).

claim: The majority of PhyB molecules were functionally active.
source: Since at photoequilibrium under 660 nm light only 80% of the PhyB molecules are in the ON state (Bae and Choi, 2008; Smith et al., 2016), we conclude that the majority of PhyB molecules were functionally active.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of the 70% complexed with the 80% theoretical maximum.

claim: Soluble TCR ligands are active as dimers.
source: Although soluble TCR ligands are active as dimers (Boniface et al., 1998; Cochran et al., 2000; Minguet and Schamel, 2008; Minguet et al., 2007), tetrameric pMHC based on streptavidin are routinely used to stimulate the TCR (Altman et al., 1996) and to obtain insight into ligand discrimination by T cells (Stone et al., 2011; Stone et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Boniface et al., 1998; Cochran et al., 2000; Minguet and Schamel, 2008; Minguet et al., 2007).

claim: Tetrameric pMHC based on streptavidin are routinely used to stimulate the TCR.
source: Although soluble TCR ligands are active as dimers (Boniface et al., 1998; Cochran et al., 2000; Minguet and Schamel, 2008; Minguet et al., 2007), tetrameric pMHC based on streptavidin are routinely used to stimulate the TCR (Altman et al., 1996) and to obtain insight into ligand discrimination by T cells (Stone et al., 2011; Stone et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Altman et al., 1996; Stone et al., 2011; Stone et al., 2001).

claim: All PIF61-100 mutants formed complexes with PhyB(660) similar to MBP-PIF(wt).
source: All mutants formed complexes with PhyB pre-illuminated with 660 nm light [PhyB(660)] similar to MBP-PIF(wt).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: PIF61-100 C9S C10S S37A [PIF(SSA)] showed the highest surface presence among the PIF-TCR constructs.
source: PIF61-100 C9S C10S S37A [PIF(SSA)] showed the highest surface presence (Figure 3B), indicating that it assembled to a complete TCR complex (Alarcón et al., 2003; Call and Wucherpfennig, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No binding of PhyBt to the PIFS-TCR on the surface of Jurkat cells could be detected.
source: Surprisingly, despite the good interaction of MBP-PIFS with PhyB in size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), no binding of PhyBt to the PIFS-TCR on the surface of Jurkat cells could be detected (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PIFS-TCR Jurkat cells could be stimulated to flux calcium via cross-linking of the PIFS-TCR using an anti-Vβ3 antibody.
source: Furthermore, PIFS-TCR Jurkat cells could be stimulated to flux calcium via cross-linking of the PIFS-TCR using an anti-Vβ3 antibody, but not using PhyBt pre-illuminated with 660 nm light, called PhyBt(660) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: PIFS-TCR Jurkat cells could not be stimulated using PhyBt(660).
source: Furthermore, PIFS-TCR Jurkat cells could be stimulated to flux calcium via cross-linking of the PIFS-TCR using an anti-Vβ3 antibody, but not using PhyBt pre-illuminated with 660 nm light, called PhyBt(660) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: PIFS loses its binding capacity towards PhyB when it is fused to the TCR and exposed on the T cell's surface.
source: Consequently, although PIFS-TCRβ is present at the cell surface and PIFS itself binds to PhyB (in the form of MBP-PIF), PIFS loses its binding capacity towards PhyB when it is fused to the TCR and exposed on the T cell's surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations described in the text.

claim: PhyBt(660) hardly bound to the surface of Jurkat cells expressing GFP-F1-PIFS-TCR or GFP-F2-PIFS-TCR with efficiently cleaved moxGFP.
source: PhyBt(660) hardly bound to the surface of Jurkat cells expressing GFP-F1-PIFS-TCR or GFP-F2-PIFS-TCR with efficiently cleaved moxGFP (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Fusing moxGFP permanently to PIFS-TCRβ resulted in strong light-dependent binding of PhyBt to the cell surface.
source: However, fusing moxGFP permanently to PIFS-TCRβ resulted in strong light-dependent binding of PhyBt to the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4E,F.

claim: moxGFP has to be present at the GFP-PIFS-TCR on the cell surface for PIFS to bind to PhyBt(660).
source: These data suggest that moxGFP has to be present at the GFP-PIFS-TCR on the cell surface, in order for PIFS to bind to PhyBt(660).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations comparing constructs with and without GFP cleavage.

claim: PhyBt(660) bound to cells expressing the GFP-PIFS-TCR, whereas PhyBt(740) did not.
source: PhyBt(660) bound to cells expressing the GFP-PIFS-TCR, whereas PhyBt pre-illuminated with 740 nm light [PhyBt(740)] did not (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Addition of PhyBt(660), but not PhyBt(740), resulted in a strong calcium influx into GFP-PIFS-TCR cells similar to stimulation using an anti-TCR antibody.
source: Binding induced TCR signaling, since addition of PhyBt(660), but not PhyBt(740), resulted in a strong calcium influx into the cells similar to a stimulation using an anti-TCR antibody (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: 660 nm light alone in the absence of PhyBt or GFP-PIFS-TCR did not evoke signaling.
source: 660 nm light alone in the absence of PhyBt or GFP-PIFS-TCR did not evoke signaling; similarly Jurkat cells not expressing the GFP-PIFS-TCR could not be stimulated with PhyBt(660) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Jurkat cells not expressing the GFP-PIFS-TCR could not be stimulated with PhyBt(660).
source: 660 nm light alone in the absence of PhyBt or GFP-PIFS-TCR did not evoke signaling; similarly Jurkat cells not expressing the GFP-PIFS-TCR could not be stimulated with PhyBt(660) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: PhyB monomers could not stimulate calcium influx in contrast to PhyB tetramers.
source: Furthermore, as seen with soluble pMHC ligands (Boniface et al., 1998; Cochran et al., 2000; Minguet et al., 2007), PhyB monomers (in contrast to tetramers) could not stimulate calcium influx (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Stimulation with bead-coupled PhyBt(660) in the dark resulted in up-regulation of the activation marker CD69.
source: Lastly, stimulation with bead-coupled PhyBt(660) in the dark resulted in up-regulation of the activation marker CD69 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Light-mediated PhyBt-binding to GFP-PIFS-TCR induced TCR signaling and T cell activation.
source: Together these data show that light-mediated PhyBt-binding to GFP-PIFS-TCR induced TCR signaling and T cell activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations described in the text and figures.

claim: A 1 s pulse of 740 nm light stopped the ongoing calcium response initially evoked by PhyBt(660).
source: When we switched PhyBt from the ON to the OFF state by a 1 s pulse of 740 nm light, we stopped the ongoing calcium response initially evoked by PhyBt(660) (Figure 5D), demonstrating that our system is reversible.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The opto-ligand-TCR system is reversible.
source: When we switched PhyBt from the ON to the OFF state by a 1 s pulse of 740 nm light, we stopped the ongoing calcium response initially evoked by PhyBt(660) (Figure 5D), demonstrating that our system is reversible.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observation that 740 nm light can stop the calcium response.

claim: Continuous high intensity (100%) 660 nm light prevented calcium influx when PhyBt(660) was added to the GFP-PIFS-TCR cells.
source: Accordingly, continuous high intensity (100%) 660 nm light prevented calcium influx when PhyBt(660) was added to the GFP-PIFS-TCR cells (Figure 6B, orange line).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: After stopping constant 660 nm illumination, PhyB molecules that were in the ON state were trapped in this state and induced a strong calcium response.
source: After 390 s the constant 660 nm illumination was stopped, so that the PhyB molecules that were in the ON state at this moment were trapped in this state. This allowed them to bind long enough to the TCR and to induce a strong calcium response (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Constant high intensity 660 nm illumination did not harm the cells.
source: This experiment also demonstrates that the constant high intensity 660 nm illumination did not harm the cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cells could still respond with calcium influx after prolonged illumination.

claim: At 4% and 2% constant 660 nm intensity, calcium influx was evoked.
source: Indeed, at 4% and 2% constant 660 nm intensity, calcium influx was evoked (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There is a threshold of the PhyB ON half-life in inducing a calcium response that is largely independent of the PhyBt concentration.
source: We observed a threshold of the PhyB ON half-life in inducing a calcium response that was largely independent of the PhyBt concentration, a crucial property of TCR ligand discrimination (McKeithan, 1995) (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The threshold half-life was at 3% 660 nm intensity.
source: This threshold half-life was at 3% 660 nm intensity.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the experimental data.

claim: The duration of the ligand-TCR interaction controls calcium signaling.
source: Thus, we were able to control TCR signaling by changing the intensity of continuous 660 nm light, suggesting that the duration of the ligand-TCR interaction controls calcium signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The calcium signal was stopped when illuminating with high intensity continuous 660 nm light (32% and 16%) during an ongoing TCR signal.
source: During this response the long binding events were changed to fast binding events by illuminating with high intensity continuous 660 nm light (32% and 16%). As expected, the calcium signal was stopped, similar as when using 740 nm light (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The calcium response was not stopped when low intensity continuous 660 nm light (2% and 4%) was used.
source: The calcium response was not stopped when low intensity continuous 660 nm light (2% and 4%) was used, where the half-life of binding is still long.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The threshold half-life of the PhyBt-GFP-PIFS-TCR interaction to maintain the calcium response was at 3% 660 nm intensity.
source: The threshold half-life of the PhyBt-GFP-PIFS-TCR interaction to maintain the calcium response was again at 3% 660 nm intensity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Only the model with KPR yielded a satisfactory fit to the PhyBt binding and calcium signaling data.
source: We fitted both mathematical models, the one with and the one without KPR, to the PhyBt binding and calcium signaling data together. Only the model with KPR yielded a satisfactory fit, and a likelihood ratio test, with the absence of KPR being the null hypothesis and the presence of KPR being the alternative hypothesis, showed highly significant support for the KPR model (p<10−6, Figure 7D,E,F and Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7D,E,F.

claim: A likelihood ratio test showed highly significant support for the KPR model (p<10−6).
source: We fitted both mathematical models, the one with and the one without KPR, to the PhyBt binding and calcium signaling data together. Only the model with KPR yielded a satisfactory fit, and a likelihood ratio test, with the absence of KPR being the null hypothesis and the presence of KPR being the alternative hypothesis, showed highly significant support for the KPR model (p<10−6, Figure 7D,E,F and Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: These findings strongly support the existence of KPR at the TCR.
source: Taken together, these findings strongly support the existence of KPR at the TCR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mathematical modeling and statistical analysis.

claim: The half-life of the PhyB ON-TCR complex varied from 40 s to 2 s over the range of light intensities used.
source: Utilizing the kinetic data, we determined the half-life of the PhyB ON-TCR complex, ln2 /(koff +ki), which varied from 40 s to 2 s over the range of light intensities used (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling and experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The threshold half-life of the bivalent PhyBt-TCR interaction (the proofreading duration τKPR) was determined to be 8 s (95% CI: 3 s, 19 s).
source: We determined the threshold half-life of the bivalent PhyBt-TCR interaction, i.e. the proofreading duration τKPR, to be 8 s (95% CI: 3 s, 19 s) (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling and statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: For a threshold half-life of bivalent binding of PhyBt to the TCR complex of 8 s, signaling from the active TCR is half-maximal.
source: Thus, for a threshold half-life of bivalent binding of PhyBt to the TCR complex of 8 s, signaling from the active TCR is half-maximal.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the mathematical modeling results.

claim: The results largely exclude the possibility of fast rebinding events.
source: Furthermore, our results largely exclude the possibility of fast rebinding events, which would have effectively prolonged the half-life of the PhyB ON-TCR complex sensed by a KPR mechanism (Aleksic et al., 2010; Govern et al., 2010) (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by analysis in Appendix 2.

claim: The opto-ligand-TCR system allows one single ligand-TCR pair to explore a wide range of different binding half-lives when changing the intensity of red light.
source: In conclusion, we engineered the opto-ligand-TCR system, in which one single ligand-TCR pair explores a wide range of different binding half-lives when changing the intensity of red light and in which other parameters of the interaction remain constant, because we have not mutated the binding interface.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental system developed in the study.

claim: Other parameters of the interaction remain constant in the opto-ligand-TCR system because the binding interface was not mutated.
source: In conclusion, we engineered the opto-ligand-TCR system, in which one single ligand-TCR pair explores a wide range of different binding half-lives when changing the intensity of red light and in which other parameters of the interaction remain constant, because we have not mutated the binding interface.
evidence: This is a key advantage of the opto-ligand-TCR system stated in the text.

claim: The opto-ligand-TCR system combined with a mathematical model shows that KPR can explain ligand discrimination by T cells.
source: Together with a mathematical model, our data show that KPR can explain ligand discrimination by T cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the Discussion.

claim: The PhyB-PIF pair enables switching ON and OFF ligand binding in less than a second.
source: Furthermore, using the PhyB-PIF pair enables switching ON and OFF ligand binding (short pulse of 660 and 740 nm light, respectively) in less than a second (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: 740 nm light actively disrupts an existing PhyB-PIF interaction, rather than preventing rebinding.
source: Importantly, we show that 740 nm light actively disrupts an existing PhyB-PIF interaction, rather than preventing rebinding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the experimental observations.

claim: The light-induced switch between both states and the light intensity-dependent change in the binding dynamics is only found with phytochromes and not with other optogenetic or synthetic systems.
source: Both features, the light-induced switch between both states and the light intensity-dependent change in the binding dynamics, is only found with phytochromes and not with other optogenetic or synthetic systems (Kolar et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Kolar et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016).

claim: The opto-ligand-TCR system was able to provoke calcium and Erk MAP kinase signaling.
source: The opto-ligand-TCR system was not only able to provoke calcium and Erk MAP kinase signaling (not shown), but also led to the stimulation of the T cell as measured by the upregulation of the activation marker CD69.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion, with calcium data shown in figures and Erk data mentioned but not shown.

claim: The opto-ligand-TCR system led to the stimulation of the T cell as measured by the upregulation of the activation marker CD69.
source: The opto-ligand-TCR system was not only able to provoke calcium and Erk MAP kinase signaling (not shown), but also led to the stimulation of the T cell as measured by the upregulation of the activation marker CD69.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The TCR can be fully stimulated in synthetic settings and not only by pMHC.
source: This is in line with systems where other binding domains were fused to the TCR (single chain Fv and DNA, (Minguet et al., 2007; Schamel and Reth, 2012; Taylor et al., 2017), indicating that the TCR can be fully stimulated in synthetic settings and not only by pMHC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and previous work cited (Minguet et al., 2007; Schamel and Reth, 2012; Taylor et al., 2017).

claim: T cells discriminate between ligands due to differences in the ligand-TCR half-lives.
source: Our opto-ligand-TCR system allowed us to show that T cells discriminate between ligands due to differences in the ligand-TCR half-lives (Figure 8), consistent with KPR models (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Davis and van der Merwe, 2006; Lever et al., 2016; McKeithan, 1995).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data and mathematical modeling shown in Figure 8.

claim: Using the identical ligand-TCR pair for the different half-lives excludes differences in binding geometry, forces or conformational changes as discriminatory parameters.
source: Using the identical ligand-TCR pair for the different half-lives excludes differences in binding geometry (Adams et al., 2011), forces (Kim et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2014) or conformational changes (Gil et al., 2002) as discriminatory parameters in this setup.
evidence: This is a key advantage of the opto-ligand-TCR system stated in the Discussion.

claim: All parameters for the mathematical model are derived using identical conditions in the opto-ligand-TCR system.
source: Furthermore, we measured total binding, the binding kinetics and the activation readout in the same experimental system. Thus, all parameters for the mathematical model are derived using identical conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of the experimental approach.

claim: Low affinity pMHC, which are non-stimulatory, lead to partial phosphorylation of CD3ζ, whereas high affinity pMHC, which are stimulatory, lead to full phosphorylation of CD3ζ.
source: Low affinity pMHC, which are non-stimulatory, lead to partial phosphorylation, whereas high affinity pMHC, which are stimulatory, lead to full phosphorylation of CD3ζ (Madrenas et al., 1995; van Oers et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Madrenas et al., 1995; van Oers et al., 1993).

claim: Increasing the concentration of low affinity binders did not lead to full CD3ζ phosphorylation.
source: Indeed, increasing the concentration of the low affinity binders did not lead to full CD3ζ phosphorylation (Madrenas et al., 1997), being consistent with KPR.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Madrenas et al., 1997).

claim: Changing the half-life of PhyB ON altered the amount of bound receptors.
source: Interestingly, changing the half-life of PhyB ON and thus the lifetime of the ligand-TCR interaction also altered the amount of bound receptors, and with the help of the mathematical model we could show that the half-life was the decisive parameter for the magnitude of T cell stimulation as measured by calcium influx.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the experimental observations and mathematical modeling.

claim: The half-life was the decisive parameter for the magnitude of T cell stimulation as measured by calcium influx.
source: Interestingly, changing the half-life of PhyB ON and thus the lifetime of the ligand-TCR interaction also altered the amount of bound receptors, and with the help of the mathematical model we could show that the half-life was the decisive parameter for the magnitude of T cell stimulation as measured by calcium influx.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mathematical modeling and experimental data.

claim: For soluble TCR ligands, bivalent binding is required to trigger the TCR.
source: For soluble TCR ligands, as we have used here, it has been shown that bivalent binding is required to trigger the TCR (Boniface et al., 1998; Cochran et al., 2000; Kaye and Janeway, 1984), possibly due to both a lack of clustering and stabilization of conformational changes of the TCR (Minguet et al., 2007; Schamel et al., 2017; Swamy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Boniface et al., 1998; Cochran et al., 2000; Kaye and Janeway, 1984; Minguet et al., 2007; Schamel et al., 2017; Swamy et al., 2016).

claim: PhyB monomers did not activate the TCR whereas PhyB tetramers did.
source: Indeed, also in our case PhyB monomers did not activate the TCR whereas PhyB tetramers (PhyBt) did.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The PhyBt ligands needed to bind for at least 8 s bivalently to stimulate calcium influx.
source: Thus, the PhyBt ligands needed to bind for at least 8 s bivalently, in order to stimulate calcium influx that itself occurred later.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mathematical modeling results.

claim: The KPR duration is not identical to the time delay between ligand binding and calcium influx or other downstream events.
source: Of note, the KPR duration is not identical to the time delay between ligand binding and calcium influx or other downstream events (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: A time delay is a prerequisite for KPR, but does not necessarily indicate that KPR takes place.
source: A time delay is a prerequisite for KPR, but does not necessarily indicate that KPR takes place.
evidence: This is a conceptual clarification stated in the Discussion.

claim: The accompanying paper by Tischer and Weiner found a KPR time of approximately 7 s.
source: In line with our 8 s KPR time, the accompanying paper by Tischer and Weiner found a KPR time of approximately 7 s (Tischer and Weiner, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the accompanying paper (Tischer and Weiner, 2019).

claim: Independent of the readout and exact design of the optogenetic system, Jurkat cells have a TCR/chimeric antigen receptor based KPR time of 7–8 s.
source: Thus, independent of the readout and exact design of the optogenetic system Jurkat cells have a TCR/-chimeric antigen receptor based KPR time of 7–8 s.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current study with the Tischer and Weiner study.

claim: Most other studies have calculated a KPR time of between 1–5 s.
source: Most other studies have calculated a KPR time of between 1–5 s (Aleksic et al., 2010; Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Daniels et al., 2006; Govern et al., 2010; Holler and Kranz, 2003; Kersh et al., 1998) and the time delay between ligand binding and calcium influx was 7 s in one study (Huse et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Aleksic et al., 2010; Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Daniels et al., 2006; Govern et al., 2010; Holler and Kranz, 2003; Kersh et al., 1998; Huse et al., 2007).

claim: The co-receptors CD4 and CD8 increase the speed of signaling, most likely by efficiently recruiting the kinase Lck to the TCR.
source: In contrast to those studies, our and the Tischer/Weiner systems lack the co-receptor CD4 and CD8 that have been shown to increase the speed of signaling, most likely by efficiently recruiting the kinase Lck to the TCR (Artyomov et al., 2010; Holler and Kranz, 2003; Veillette et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Artyomov et al., 2010; Holler and Kranz, 2003; Veillette et al., 1988).

claim: Differences in the cellular background might contribute to differences in the KPR time.
source: Differences in the cellular background (primary murine T cells versus the human T cell line Jurkat) might also contribute to differences in the KPR time, e.g., if the concentration of kinases or phosphatases was different (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005).
evidence: This is speculation stated in the Discussion, with a citation to support the general concept (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005).

claim: Individual binding events longer than the threshold half-life might be the ones that triggered T cell activation.
source: The half-life of the interaction is a population average over many binding events. Thus, it might be that individual binding events longer than the threshold half-life (8 s in our case) are the ones that triggered T cell activation, as suggested recently (Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation stated in the Discussion, with a citation to support the idea (Lin et al., 2019).

claim: The on-rate in the opto-ligand-TCR system seems to be too slow to significantly contribute to fast rebinding effects.
source: However, the on-rate in our opto-ligand-TCR system seems to be too slow to significantly contribute to this effect (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by analysis in Appendix 2.

claim: The rate of converting PhyB from ON to OFF is the same for free PhyB and PIF-bound PhyB.
source: In support of the model (Figure 7A), we experimentally demonstrated that the rate of converting PhyB from ON to OFF is the same for free PhyB and PIF-bound PhyB (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: PhyB molecules convert to OFF while being bound to PIF and thereby the PhyB-PIF interaction is lost.
source: These data imply that PhyB molecules also convert to OFF while being bound to PIF and thereby the PhyB-PIF interaction is lost.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The effective off-rate and binding affinity of PhyB ON to the TCR are light-dependent.
source: Hence, the effective off-rate and binding affinity of PhyB ON to the TCR are also light-dependent (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model and experimental observations, illustrated in Figure 7B,C.

claim: The amount of TCR-bound PhyB decreases with increasing light intensity.
source: Taken together, the model predicts that the amount of TCR-bound PhyB decreases with increasing light intensity, which we confirmed experimentally (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The change of PhyB ON affinity is a straightforward consequence of the light-controlled PhyB ON half-life.
source: Importantly, the change of PhyB ON affinity is a straightforward consequence of the light-controlled PhyB ON half-life (this contrasts with mutated pMHC ligands (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Daniels et al., 2006; Davis and van der Merwe, 2006; Holler and Kranz, 2003; Lever et al., 2016), where affinity changes can be brought about by changes in both on- and off-rates, and potentially other parameters such as orientation of binding (Adams et al., 2011)).
evidence: This is a key advantage of the opto-ligand-TCR system stated in the Results, contrasting it with previous approaches.

claim: Bivalent binding is required to activate the TCR when using soluble TCR ligands.
source: We used a soluble TCR ligand for which - in case of antibodies or pMHC - it was shown that bivalent binding is required to activate the TCR (Boniface et al., 1998; Cochran et al., 2000; Kaye and Janeway, 1984; Minguet et al., 2007), and this most likely was also the case for our opto-ligand-TCR system (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The KPR duration in the opto-ligand-TCR system is the time from bivalent binding to the completion of the biochemical signaling steps.
source: Thus, the KPR duration in our system is the time from bivalent binding to the completion of the biochemical signaling steps (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and illustrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.
